title: Bach's musical signature
hook: Johann Sebastian Bach could spell his own surname in musical notes.
peek: In German, the note we call B-flat is written B, and B-natural is written H. That quirk let Johann Sebastian Bach spell his surname as four notes, a twisting little motif that composers from Schumann to Pärt have borrowed ever since.
lede: English speakers name notes A to G. German musicians use the same letters with one twist: what English calls B-flat is B in German, and B-natural is H. So the surname BACH becomes four real notes: B-flat, A, C, B-natural. Johann Sebastian Bach knew it, worked the motif into his music, and it became music's most famous signature.

bullets.text: Medieval scribes wrote two kinds of B: a rounded b for the flat version and a square b for the natural. Over time the square form was read as the letter h, and German note names kept it.
Bach worked his name into the last fugue of The Art of Fugue, a set of studies he left unfinished. The B-A-C-H motif enters as a new theme shortly before the manuscript breaks off.

Played in order, the four notes huddle together and twist back on themselves, a tight chromatic knot. That compact, slightly uneasy shape makes it easy to hide inside other music and easy for listeners to spot.
Later composers paid tribute with it. Liszt wrote a Fantasy and Fugue on B-A-C-H for organ, Schumann composed six fugues on the name, and Arvo Pärt built his 1964 piece Collage on B-A-C-H around it.
